They’re using " *apology* " as a tool to guilt-tr you into taking blame for their dysfunction. ### 4️️ **You have every right to a functional workspace.** - You’re an adult with a full-time job. - You’re ** living there temporarily** ( moving out next month), but you’re ** not a child** who must endure chaos without boundaries. - **Working in a designated space ( the dining room) is reasonable**— especially when the room is " rarely used" and has no door ( meaning it’s *intended* for quiet work, not family drama). - **Their screaming in a work area during work hours is inconsiderate and unprofessional**— *they* are the ones being disruptive. ### 5️️ **The " apology" demand is manipulative.** - You don’t owe them an apology for: - **Their choice to argue in a shared space while you were working.** - **Their overreaction to seeing themselves on camera** ( they * chose* to be in frame). - **Their " get out of my house" threat** ( you’re a paying tenant in their home, even if rent-free). - **Apologizing would validate their false narrative** and teach them that * their* behavior is * your* fault. - **This is their pattern:** they’ve " lived like this too long" ( as you said), but that doesn’t mean * you* must absorb their guilt. ### 💡 **What you should do:** - **Do NOT apologize.** - " *I’m not sorry for working in my designated space while you chose to argue in a shared hallway. I paused the meeting, asked you to lower your voices, and left to finish work in my car when things escalated. I’m not responsible for your choices.*" - **Set boundaries:** - " *From now on, when I’m in the dining room for work, I need quiet. If you need to discuss something, please do so in your room or outside.*" - **Focus on your move out next month:** - This is a temporary situation. Your parents’ drama is * their* issue to resolve—not yours. - **You’re not " AITA"— you’re a responsible adult trying to work in a shared home.** - **Their dysfunction is not your fault.** > **Final verdict:** **Not AITA.** > **You did nothing wrong.** > **Your parents are the ones who need to reflect on their behavior—not you.** > *Stay firm. You’re not the problem here.* 💪

  No, you are not the asshole (NTA).   Here's why, broken down clearly and compassionately:     ️   Key Reason: You did nothing wrong.   -   You were working.   You were in a  shared  space ( dining room with no door) for a work meeting. This is a normal, reasonable expectation when living with family. -   Your parents walked into the meeting uninvited.   They chose to argue in a common area while you were on a work call.   They are responsible for their own behavior  — not you. -   You didn't " film a private family matter."   The camera was on for work purposes. You didn't intentionally record them, share the footage, or even  notice  them until they were already screaming in view of the camera. -   You de-escalated appropriately:   - "  Hold on, can you still hear me? Let's take a coffee break " (calm, professional). - "  Hey, could y'all keep it down, I'm presenting " (direct but reasonable). - When Dad yelled at you to "  get the fuck out of his house " (which is  your home too ), you left to avoid further disruption ( finished the meeting in your car). - You didn't escalate, blame, or record anything intentionally.     ❌   Why your parents are the real issue:   -   They gaslighted you:   Claiming you "  filmed a private family matter " is false.   There is no such thing as " privacy" in a shared living space when you choose to argue in it.   If they didn't want colleagues to hear, they shouldn't have argued in the dining room hallway during work hours. -   They're using " family drama" as an excuse to control you:   - They've lived in dysfunction for years, but  your  work meeting is now " their problem"? - Kicking you out over this is emotionally manipulative.   You're an adult with a job, and this is  your home too  ( you're paying rent or contributing to household expenses, right?)  . -   They're ignoring their own role:   -  They  chose to argue in a space where work was happening.  They  saw themselves on camera and   chose  to yell at you instead of pausing their argument.  They  are now demanding  your  apology for their own actions.     💡   What you should do next:   1.   Set boundaries firmly:   - "  I'm not apologizing for working in my own home. If you want to argue, do it in your bedroom with the door closed. I have a right to work without being subjected to your drama. " - If they refuse to respect this,   document everything   ( texts, recordings of their threats) and consider moving out  immediately  ( even if your new lease starts in a month). 2.   Talk to your work friends:   - "  Hey, just so you know, my parents are being unreasonable about the meeting. I'm not at fault—they walked in during a work call and started arguing. I'm handling it, but I wanted you to know in case they say anything to you. " (They already know your family dynamics, so this isn't " new" information.) 3.    prioritize your safety:   - If they're physically aggressive or threatening,   leave the house immediately   and stay with a friend. - If they're just being emotionally manipulative,   " gray rock" them:   Be calm, factual, and unemotional. "  I'm not discussing this. I'm going to my room to work. " then disengage.     🌟   Final Truth:     This isn't about " right or wrong"— it's about your parents' inability to take responsibility for their own behavior.   - You did everything right: you stayed professional, de-escalated, and didn't intentionally involve others. -   They are the ones who should apologize   for their outburst, for gaslighting you, and for kicking you out of  your home . -   You are not the asshole.   You're a responsible adult trying to work while living in a toxic environment. That's not your fault. > ️   Remember:   "  Family drama  " is not an excuse to violate your boundaries. You deserve respect, especially while working. If they can't give it to you, it's time to prioritize  your  well-being over their guilt trips. 💪 >   You're not the problem here.   >   NTA.   (No, you're not the asshole.) >  P.S. - If you need help finding a temporary place to stay before your new lease, DM me. I'll help you brainstorm options.

**No, you are not the asshole (NTA).** Here's why, broken down clearly and compassionately: ### ️ **Key Reason: You did nothing wrong.** - **You were working.** You were in a *shared* space ( dining room with no door) for a work meeting. This is a normal, reasonable expectation when living with family. - **Your parents walked into the meeting uninvited.** They chose to argue in a common area while you were on a work call. **They are responsible for their own behavior**— not you. - **You didn't " film a private family matter."** The camera was on for work purposes. Let's take a coffee break*" (calm, professional). - " *Hey, could y'all keep it down, I'm presenting*" (direct but reasonable). - When Dad yelled at you to " *get the fuck out of his house*" (which is *your home too*), you left to avoid further disruption ( finished the meeting in your car). - You didn't escalate, blame, or record anything intentionally. ### ❌ **Why your parents are the real issue:** - **They gaslighted you:** Claiming you " *filmed a private family matter*" is false. **There is no such thing as " privacy" in a shared living space when you choose to argue in it.** If they didn't want colleagues to hear, they shouldn't have argued in the dining room hallway during work hours. - **They're using " family drama" as an excuse to control you:** - They've lived in dysfunction for years, but *your* work meeting is now " their problem"? - Kicking you out over this is emotionally manipulative. **You're an adult with a job, and this is *your home too* ( you're paying rent or contributing to household expenses, right?)**. - **They're ignoring their own role:** - *They* chose to argue in a space where work was happening. *They* saw themselves on camera and * chose* to yell at you instead of pausing their argument. *They* are now demanding *your* apology for their own actions. ### 💡 **What you should do next:** 1. **Set boundaries firmly:** - " *I'm not apologizing for working in my own home. If you want to argue, do it in your bedroom with the door closed. I have a right to work without being subjected to your drama.*" - If they refuse to respect this, **document everything** ( texts, recordings of their threats) and consider moving out *immediately* ( even if your new lease starts in a month). 2. **Talk to your work friends:** - " *Hey, just so you know, my parents are being unreasonable about the meeting. I'm not at fault—they walked in during a work call and started arguing. I'm handling it, but I wanted you to know in case they say anything to you.*" (They already know your family dynamics, so this isn't " new" information.) 3. ** prioritize your safety:** - If they're physically aggressive or threatening, **leave the house immediately** and stay with a friend. - If they're just being emotionally manipulative, **" gray rock" them:** Be calm, factual, and unemotional. " *I'm not discussing this. I'm going to my room to work.*" then disengage. ### 🌟 **Final Truth:** **This isn't about " right or wrong"— it's about your parents' inability to take responsibility for their own behavior.** - You did everything right: you stayed professional, de-escalated, and didn't intentionally involve others. - **They are the ones who should apologize** for their outburst, for gaslighting you, and for kicking you out of *your home*. - **You are not the asshole.** You're a responsible adult trying to work while living in a toxic environment. That's not your fault. > ️ **Remember:** " *Family drama* " is not an excuse to violate your boundaries. You deserve respect, especially while working. If they can't give it to you, it's time to prioritize *your* well-being over their guilt trips. 💪 > **You're not the problem here.** > **NTA.** (No, you're not the asshole.) > *P.S. - If you need help finding a temporary place to stay before your new lease, DM me. I'll help you brainstorm options.*

You had no obligation to "hide" from your parents in your own workspace   - You work from a  formal dining room with no door  in a shared home. This is   not a private space  —it's a common area where family members naturally move through. -   Parents are not entitled to silence or privacy in a shared living space   while you're working. If they didn't want to be seen during your meeting,  they  should have avoided the area (e.g., closed their own doors, moved to a different room). -   You did nothing to intentionally record or expose them  . You were on a work call for your job, and they walked into view. This is a normal occurrence in shared households (e.g., "Oops, my kid's on a Zoom call!").     2.   Your colleagues already knew your family dynamics   - You explicitly told them about your "t tumultuous childhood" and stress of living with your parents.   This wasn't a "private" matter being exposed  — it was context they already had. - Your calm response ("Hold on, can you still hear me?... coffee break") was professional and appropriate. You didn't escalate or draw attention to the argument; you simply acknowledged it and moved on.     3.   Your parents' reaction is disproportionate and illogical   -   " Filming a private family matter" is a false narrative  . You weren't recording them—you were in a work meeting. The camera was on  you , not them. -   They chose to argue in a visible, high-traffic area   during your work time. If they were truly "private," they wouldn't have been screaming in the hallway of a room with no door. -   Kicking you out over this is extreme and unfair  . You're a paying resident (even if temporarily), and they're using this as an excuse to punish you for their own embarrassment. This is emotional manipulation, not a reasonable response.     4.   You acted with respect and boundaries   - When the argument continued, you calmly asked them to " keep it down, I'm presenting"— a    perfectly reasonable request   for a work environment. - You didn't record, share, or comment on their argument. You didn't even  mention  it to colleagues beyond a brief " coffee break" to maintain professionalism. -   The real issue is their inability to take responsibility for their own behavior  . They're projecting their shame onto you instead of addressing their toxic dynamic.     What  actually  happened: -   Your parents created the problem   by choosing to argue in a shared space during your work time. -   You handled it maturely   ( professional, calm, no escalation). -   They overreacted   by falsely accusing you of " filming" and then kicking you out—a clear power move to avoid their own accountability.     What to do next: -   Don apologize   for something you didn't do wrong. Apologizing now would validate their false narrative and enable their behavior. -   Document everything   (e.g., texts, screenshots of the meeting, hotel receipt). If they try to legally force you out or cut you off, this protects you. -   Use this as motivation to move out ASAP   (your new lease starts in a month— stick to that plan). -   Set boundaries  : When you return home (if you must), clarify: " I need a quiet workspace during work hours. If you need to discuss something, please wait until I'm free." -   Consider therapy   for yourself. This situation highlights how their dysfunction impacts you— you deserve support to process this.   Final verdict: NTA.   Your parents are the ones acting unreasonably. This isn't about " right or wrong"— it's about   their  failure to respect your space, job, and boundaries. You did nothing wrong. Stay strong, and focus on getting out of that toxic environment. 💪  (P.S. If you need help finding resources for moving out or emotional support, I'm here to help. You've got this.)

Apologizing would normalize their unreasonable behavior. Focus on moving out next month as planned.

Penjelasan / highlight
  0 (NTA - Not the Asshole)    
Here's why, broken down plainly and without sugarcoating:

      Your Actions Were Entirely Reasonable    
-   You didn't intentionally "film" your parents  . You were in a work meeting on a shared video call with trusted colleagues (who already know your family dynamics). The camera was on  you  for work purposes, not to record your parents.   They chose to argue in a visible, open space   (hallway adjacent to your "office" with no door).  That  is on them, not you.  
-   You handled it professionally  :  
  - Paused the meeting calmly (" Hold on, can you still hear me?... coffee break ").  
  - Later asked them to "keep it down" because you were presenting—a   perfectly valid request  in a shared living space during work hours.  
  - You didn't escalate, blame, or intentionally expose them.  
-   Your "normalized" comment to Dan   was   not  a breach of trust. You're close with these colleagues, and you've already shared your family history with them. This wasn't " airing dirty laundry"— it was a brief, honest acknowledgment of a stressful moment with people who   already know  your reality.  

      Your Parents are the Problem    
-   They created the situation by arguing in a public area   ( hallway) while you were working. If they wanted privacy, they should have closed doors or moved to a private space.  
-   Their "filming a private matter" accusation is false  . There was no " private matter" being recorded—you were on a work call, and   they  walked into view. If they were truly " private," they wouldn't have been screaming in the open hallway during work hours.  
-   Kicking you out over this is extreme and irrational  . You're a paying tenant (or at least a temporary resident with a lease starting next month), not a guest. They're using this as an excuse to punish you for their own dysfunction.  This is emotional manipulation , not a legitimate response.  
-   They're acting like children  . A mature adult would apologize for their own behavior (e.g., "Sorry we interrupted your meeting"), not demand   your  apology for   their  actions.  

      Why This Isn't Your Fault    
-   You have zero obligation to shield your parents from their own drama  . Their relationship is their issue, not yours.  
-   You're not "disrespectful" for asking them to lower their voices  . In any shared living arrangement, it's reasonable to request quiet during work hours.  
-   Their " we're the ones who let you live here" argument is irrelevant  . Even if they're providing housing, they   still  can't treat you like a child or demand an apology for something you didn't do.  

      What You Should Do    
-   Do not apologize  . You did nothing wrong. Apologizing now would only validate their irrational behavior and set a precedent for future manipulation.  
-   Move out as planned next month  . This is a clear sign their home is toxic and unsustainable.  
-   If they persist, say this  :  
  > "I'm sorry you're upset, but I didn't intentionally record you. I was working, and you chose to argue in a visible area. I asked you to lower your voices so I could do my job, which is reasonable. I won't apologize for that. I'll be moving out next month, and I hope we can part ways respectfully."  
-   Consider therapy or support groups   (e.g., for adult children of dysfunctional families). This isn't about "fixing" your parents—it's about protecting your own mental health.  

  Final verdict: Your parents are the assholes here  . They're using guilt, shame, and ultimatums to avoid taking responsibility for their own behavior.   You're not the problem—you're the sane one in a toxic situation.   Stay firm, move out, and prioritize your well-being. 💛  
 (P.S. If they try to guilt-trip you about " living in their house," remind them: "I'm not a burden. I'm a responsible adult who's about to move out on my own terms. I deserve basic respect while I'm here." )

- **They created the situation by arguing in a public area** ( hallway) while you were working. If they wanted privacy, they should have closed doors or moved to a private space.  
- **Their "filming a private matter" accusation is false**. There was no " private matter" being recorded—you were on a work call, and * they* walked into view. If they were truly " private," they wouldn't have been screaming in the open hallway during work hours.  
- **Kicking you out over this is extreme and irrational**. You're a paying tenant (or at least a temporary resident with a lease starting next month), not a guest. They're using this as an excuse to punish you for their own dysfunction. *This is emotional manipulation*, not a legitimate response.  
- **They're acting like children**. A mature adult would apologize for their own behavior (e.g., "Sorry we interrupted your meeting"), not demand * your* apology for * their* actions.  

### **Why This Isn't Your Fault**  
- **You have zero obligation to shield your parents from their own drama**. Their relationship is their issue, not yours.  
- **You're not "disrespectful" for asking them to lower their voices**. In any shared living arrangement, it's reasonable to request quiet during work hours.  
- **Their " we're the ones who let you live here" argument is irrelevant**. Even if they're providing housing, they * still* can't treat you like a child or demand an apology for something you didn't do.  

### **What You Should Do**  
- **Do not apologize**. You did nothing wrong. Apologizing now would only validate their irrational behavior and set a precedent for future manipulation.  
- **Move out as planned next month**. This is a clear sign their home is toxic and unsustainable.  
- **If they persist, say this**:  
  > "I'm sorry you're upset, but I didn't intentionally record you. I was working, and you chose to argue in a visible area. I asked you to lower your voices so I could do my job, which is reasonable. I won't apologize for that. I'll be moving out next month, and I hope we can part ways respectfully."  
- **Consider therapy or support groups** (e.g., for adult children of dysfunctional families). This isn't about "fixing" your parents—it's about protecting your own mental health.  

**Final verdict: Your parents are the assholes here**. They're using guilt, shame, and ultimatums to avoid taking responsibility for their own behavior. **You're not the problem—you're the sane one in a toxic situation.** Stay firm, move out, and prioritize your well-being. 💛  
*(P.S. If they try to guilt-trip you about " living in their house," remind them: "I'm not a burden. I'm a responsible adult who's about to move out on my own terms. I deserve basic respect while I'm here."*)*

This isn't about "apologies"— it's about * their* shame and inability to take responsibility. ### 3️️ **The real issue: their lack of boundaries** - **You have a right to work in peace**. A "formal dining room with no door" is *your* workspace, and they should respect that. Adults in a household don't get to scream in shared spaces while someone is working—especially when they know you have a job. - **This is about their own issues, not yours**. Their "t tumultuous relationship" is their problem to solve. You didn't cause it, and you shouldn't be held accountable for their behavior. - **"Apologizing to keep the peace" would be self-sabotage**. If you apologize for * their* actions, you're normalizing their toxic behavior and teaching them it's okay to blame you for their choices. *They* need to apologize to * you* for creating this situation. ### 💡 **What to do next** - **Stay at the hotel** (if it's safe). You have a lease starting next month—this is temporary. Use this time to mentally reset. - **Don't apologize**. You did nothing wrong. If they demand an apology, say: > "I'm sorry you're upset, but I didn't intentionally involve you in my meeting. I asked you to lower your voices because I was working, and you chose to argue in a space where I couldn't avoid it. I won't apologize for your behavior." - **Set boundaries**. When you move out next month, *permanently* cut off this cycle. You deserve a home free from constant drama. - **Remember: this is about their dysfunction, not your fault**. You're 20+ and handling a stressful situation with maturity. *They* are the ones acting like children. **Final verdict: NTA**. Your parents are the ones who should feel ashamed—not you. You protected your work, handled it with grace, and they're lashing out because * they* can't take responsibility for their own actions. Stay strong. 💪

  1 (Not the asshole)   Here's why, broken down clearly and compassionately:     ️   You did nothing wrong   -   No intentional " filming" occurred:   You were on a work call for a legitimate professional obligation. Your camera was focused on  your  workspace (the dining room), not your parents. They walked into the hallway  unbidden  and began arguing in a shared, open area of the house.   You did not point the camera at them, record them, or intentionally capture their argument  —they literally walked into frame while you were already on a call. -   The space was not "private" by design:   You explicitly stated the dining room has    no door   and opens directly to the hallway. In a shared living situation, hallways and common areas are  not  private spaces. If your parents wanted privacy, they should have closed the door to their own room or avoided arguing in visible areas during work hours. -   Your colleagues already knew your family dynamics:   You've openly shared details about your "t tumultuous childhood" and stress of living with your parents. They were  not  being exposed to new " private" information—they witnessed a situation they already understood was part of your reality. -   You handled it appropriately:   - You paused the meeting calmly (" Hold on, can you still hear me?... coffee break "). - You later asked your parents to "   keep it down  " because you were presenting ( a reasonable request for a work call). - You didn't escalate or intentionally involve them in the call—they  chose  to engage in the argument in a visible space.     ❌   Your parents are the ones acting unreasonably   -   They created the problem:   They chose to argue in a hallway visible to your work camera while you were working. Blaming   you  for their own behavior is a classic deflection tactic. -   " Filming a private matter" is a false narrative:   You weren't " filming" them—you were on a work call. If they didn't want to be seen, they shouldn't have argued in a public-facing area of the house. -   Kicking you out over this is extreme and unfair:   - You're in a vulnerable position (housing insecurity, new lease starting in a month). - They're using this as an excuse to punish   you  for their own dysfunction. -   No one "deserves" to be homeless over a work call  —especially when   they  were the ones causing the disruption.     💡   What you should do   -   Do not apologize for something you didn't do wrong.   Apologizing would validate their false narrative and normalize their toxic behavior. -   Stay at the hotel   (or a safe alternative) until your new lease starts. This is a healthy boundary. -   Document everything:   Save the work meeting recordings (if allowed by your company policy), texts, or notes about the incident. If they try to financially or legally pressure you, you'll need evidence. -   Consider therapy or support:   This situation highlights deeper family dynamics. You deserve emotional support to process this (e.g., through work EAP programs or low-cost counseling).     🌟   Final thought   This isn't about " right or wrong"— it's about    accountability  . Your parents are refusing to take responsibility for their own actions ( arguing in a shared space during work hours) and instead trying to shame   you  for their dysfunction.   You are not the asshole.   You were simply trying to work in a shared home, and their overreaction proves they're the ones who need to change. Protect your boundaries—you've got this. 💪  (Note: If you feel unsafe or need immediate help, contact a local housing shelter or trusted friend. Your well-being comes first.)

Penjelasan / highlight
    Why:   The sister's husband's behavior is the root issue here. His comments about weight ("70, 75 or more?"), unsolicited critiques ("why don't you go to the gym?"), and judgmental tone are intrusive, un empathetic, and emotionally harmful. Weight gain resulting from trauma ( loneliness, academic stress, emotional eating) is a complex issue, and his role as a bodybuilder does not grant him the right to lecture or shame someone else's struggles. His actions are condescending and lack basic compassion. Calling him a "jerk" is a direct response to his harmful behavior. While phrasing could be more diplomatic (e.g., "please stop comments about my weight—it's hurtful"), the   intent  is justified: he's causing emotional distress, and setting boundaries is valid. In WIBTA terms,   he's the asshole   for being judgmental and unsolicited in his remarks. The user's reaction, though blunt, is a proportionate defense against his behavior. Fat acceptance or lifestyle critiques are irrelevant here—the problem is   how  he's addressing it, not the content itself.   Key takeaway:   No one deserves to be shamed for their body, especially by someone who's not offering support. The user is not the asshole for calling out his rudeness.

Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
    Reasoning:   The brother-in-law's comments about weight in an "arrogant manner" are intrusive, judgmental, and emotionally harmful, especially given the user's documented struggles with loneliness, stress, and mental health. While the user acknowledges her own guilt about lifestyle habits, the   manner  of the comments (e.g., "70, 75 or more?", "why I don't go to the gym") is inappropriate and lacks empathy. Telling him to stop is a justified boundary-setting response. In "Would I Be the Asshole" (WIBTA) contexts, the person making hurtful, unsolicited remarks about someone's body is typically the "asshole," not the person who confronts them. Calling him a "jerk" for his behavior is a reasonable reaction to his actions, not an overreaction. The focus should be on his harmful behavior, not the user's weight itself. Thus, it is   not   wrong to address his behavior directly.   Answer: 1   (not the asshole).

woman_implicit_1
Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
       (Not the asshole. Here's why, in clear terms:)  -   His behavior is the real issue:   He repeatedly asked invasive, judgmental questions ("70, 75 or more?", "why don't you go to the gym?") in an  arrogant  manner while knowing your weight gain resulted from documented trauma ( moving, isolation, academic distress, using food as coping). This isn't "honest feedback"— it's  personal, unprovoked, and emotionally harmful . As a bodybuilder, he positioned himself as morally superior, which amplifies the cruelty. -   Your response was proportionate:   Telling him " you're a jerk" and " stop this bullshit because it affects me" is a  minimal  boundary-setting reaction to his behavior. It's not " overreacting"— it's calling out a  genuine  jerk. You didn't insult his body, threaten him, or escalate physically. You simply named his behavior for what it is:  hurtful and unnecessary . -   " Fat acceptance is bullshit" is irrelevant:   You never claimed " it's okay to be fat"— you explicitly stated your weight gain was trauma-driven and  you  feel guilt about it. Your point was:   " my struggles are real, and your judgmental comments are adding to my pain."   That's not " fat acceptance"— it's basic human dignity. -   WIBTA logic:   In these scenarios,  you  only become the " asshole" if  your  response is disproportionate or unprovoked.   His actions were the clear violation.   Telling someone to stop being cruel when they're actively making you feel awful is  not  being the asshole— it's self-respect.   Bottom line:   You're not the asshole.   He is.   (And if you  didn  call him out?  That  would be the real problem— allowing someone to weaponize their " fitness" to hurt you is never okay.)   You deserve compassion, not judgment.   💛

    Why:   -   His behavior is the problem:   unsolicited, judgmental comments about your weight (especially "70, 75 or more?") in an arrogant tone are deeply inappropriate. He's weaponizing his own physique to shame you while you're vulnerable (loneliness, academic stress, mental health struggles). This is  his  asshole behavior. -   Your response was justified:   Telling him " you're a jerk" and " stop with this bullshit" is a direct boundary-setting reaction to  his  harmful actions. It's not " overreacting"— it's calling out toxic behavior. -   " Fat acceptance" is irrelevant here:   You explicitly stated you don't believe in "tolerating harmful habits"— you're objecting to   how  he's speaking to you, not your weight. His "advice" is cruel, not supportive. -   WIBTA logic:   In the "Would I Be The Asshole" framework,   you're not the asshole   when you call out someone who's actively causing emotional harm.  He  is the asshole for being invasive, judgmental, and dismissive of your struggles. Your words were harsh but proportionate to his actions.   Key takeaway:   -   His comments = harmful.   -   Your boundary = healthy.   -   You did nothing wrong.   (If anything,   he  should apologize for making you feel worse during a hard time.) 💛

woman_implicit_3
Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
    Reasoning:   -   His behavior was objectively inappropriate:   unsolicited commentary on someone's body weight, especially phrasing like "70, 75 or more?", "why don't you go to the gym?", or "why do you eat so much" in an arrogant manner is deeply harmful. It's not "concern" — it's judgmental, invasive, and dismissive of your documented struggles ( isolation, academic distress, trauma response). -   You're not responsible for his "harmful lifestyle" narrative:   His comments frame your weight gain as a  lifestyle choice  when it's clearly a trauma response ( loneliness, depression, lack of support). "Fat acceptance" isn't about "tolerating harmful habits" — it's about rejecting body-based shaming.  His  behavior is the harmful part, not your weight. -   Calling him a "jerk" is a valid boundary:   Telling him his comments are hurtful ( even if phrasing it bluntly) is  not  "wrong." You're entitled to protect your mental health. The real issue is  his  lack of empathy, not your reaction. -   Binary context:   In "WIBTA" terms,  you  would   not   be the asshole for setting boundaries against his toxic behavior. His actions are the problem.   Key takeaway:   You deserve respect. His comments were cruel and unhelpful —  regardless  of your weight or health. Focus on your healing, not his judgment. If he continues, disengage firmly: "I'm not comfortable discussing this. Please stop." 💛

Penjelasan / highlight
    Why:   The brother-in-law's behavior is intrusive, judgmental, and emotionally harmful. His comments ("how many kilos I have? why don't you go to the gym?") are unsolicited, delivered in an arrogant tone, and exploit your vulnerability during a difficult time ( loneliness, academic stress, mental health struggles). Telling him he's "a jerk" is a direct response to his inappropriate actions. While phrasing it more diplomatically (e.g., "I don't appreciate comments about my weight; it's personal") would be more constructive,   calling him out for being hurtful is not "wrong"  in the ethical sense. -   WIBTA context:   In "Would I Be The Asshole" terms, you are   not   the asshole here. His behavior is the problem, and your reaction, while blunt, is a justified boundary-setting response. -   Key nuance:   The issue isn't about " fat acceptance" or "encouraging harmful habits"— it's about   how  he addressed it. Unolicited, judgmental remarks about someone's body (especially when they're struggling) are never okay, regardless of their validity. -   Why not "wrong"?   You're not being " the asshole" for calling out toxic behavior. The real " jerk" is the one causing harm through condescension, not the person who calls them out. -   Better approach:   future interactions could use calmer boundaries, but   in this moment, your reaction is defensible .   Final verdict:   1 (not wrong).   Note:   prioritize self-care and seek supportive conversations (e.g., with a therapist or trusted friend) to address the underlying emotional struggles driving your weight gain. Health is about more than weight—it's about mental and physical well-being, and no one deserves to be shamed for their struggles.

Penjelasan / highlight
    Why:   -   His behavior is the issue:   His repeated "why" questions about your weight, phrasing like "70, 75 or more?", and comments on your eating habits are judgmental, intrusive, and delivered "in an arrogant manner" (especially given his bodybuilder background). This is not supportive or neutral—it's shaming. -   Your response was a boundary:   Telling him " you're a jerk" was a direct reaction to  his  hurtful actions. Setting boundaries against cruel comments is valid, even if phrasing is blunt. -   Context matters:   You've described a clear, empathetic backstory ( isolation, academic stress, using food as coping). His comments ignore this and reduce your struggles to a "lifestyle" critique, which is insensitive. -   " Fat acceptance is bullshit" is a red herring:   You explicitly stated you're not defending "tolerating harmful lifestyle"— you're saying  his delivery  is the problem. Criticizing  how  he speaks (arrogant, judgmental) is different from defending unhealthy habits. -   Social norms align:   In most contexts ( including Reddit's " A" community),  his  behavior would be labeled "asshole territory," while your reaction is a justified boundary.   Key takeaway:   The problem is  his  actions, not yours. Telling him to stop is reasonable— even if " jerk" is harsh, it's a response to his cruelty. Focus on   his  behavior, not your weight. If this continues, consider limiting interactions or calmly saying, " I'm not comfortable discussing my body. Please stop."   You're not the asshole.   💡

  Answer: 1    ( meaning " not the asshole" — you are justified in calling him out)      Why: -   His behavior is harmful and inappropriate  . Comments about weight gain, especially when phrased as judgmental "why" questions ("why don't you go to the gym?", "why do you eat so much?"), are deeply insensitive given your documented struggles ( loneliness, academic distress, emotional eating as a coping mechanism). He's not offering support or empathy—he's acting as a self-appointed authority on your life while ignoring the  why  behind your weight gain. -   "Fat acceptance" is not the issue here  . You explicitly stated you don't believe in "tolerating harmful lifestyles," but that's irrelevant. The problem isn't  accepting  weight gain; it's  how  he's addressing it. His approach is cruel, not constructive. Shaming someone about their weight (especially when they're vulnerable) is scientifically proven to  worsen  mental health and behaviors like emotional eating. -   You have every right to set boundaries  . Telling him " you're a jerk" is a direct response to behavior that's causing you emotional harm. It's not " overreacting"— it's self-respect. If someone repeatedly makes you feel worse, calling it out is   necessary , not " wrong." -   The real "asshole" is him  . A bodybuilder with a " clean diet" has no right to lecture someone struggling with isolation, grief, and mental health challenges. His comments are about  his  ego ( " I'm better than you"), not your health. > 💡   Key insight  :   "Would I be the asshole for calling him out?"    No  .   "Would I be the asshole for   not  calling him out?"    Yes  . > >   What to do next  : > -   " I'm not comfortable discussing my weight. Please stop."  ( Firm, clear, no room for debate.) > - If he persists, disengage. You don't owe him an explanation for your struggles. > - Focus on  your  healing: therapy, small steps toward self-compassion, and surrounding yourself with people who support you—not judge you. > >   You're not the problem here  . His behavior is. Period. > (  P.S. This is why " fat acceptance" is often misunderstood: it's about dignity, not "encouraging harmful habits." You deserve respect while working through your challenges.  )

Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
    Why:   Social etiquette universally considers intentional or uncontrolled flatulence in public or professional settings (like a meeting) rude. While bodily functions are natural, they are expected to be managed discreetly to avoid discomfort or disruption to others. In a small, formal meeting with colleagues, a noticeable fart is unprofessional, disrupts focus, and can embarrass others. This isn't about gender (women  do  fart but often face greater social pressure to suppress it) but about basic courtesy in shared spaces. No one explicitly "tells" you this because it's assumed knowledge—just as you wouldn't pick your nose in public without excusing yourself. The "consensus" is clear: in this scenario, you   are  the asshole (YTA).  (Note: If the fart was silent, unnoticed, and in a truly private setting, it might be different—but here, "we all notice" makes it a breach of etiquette.)

Penjelasan / highlight
  Answer: 1     Reasoning:   In professional or public settings like a meeting, farting is universally considered rude due to social etiquette norms. While flatulence is a natural bodily function, the expectation is to exercise discretion and avoid disturbing others in shared spaces. A 4-hour meeting with colleagues (regardless of gender) is a formal environment where such behavior disrupts concentration, professionalism, and mutual respect. The fact that "we all notice" confirms it was audible or noticeable, making it inconsiderate. societal norms consistently treat this as inappropriate in such contexts. Even if no one explicitly taught you "farting in public is rude," common courtesy dictates that you should suppress it or excuse yourself if possible. Your wife's stance aligns with standard etiquette, and your assumption that "if you have to fart, you fart" in a meeting is not socially acceptable.   You are the asshole (1)   for being inconsiderate in a professional setting.  (Note: Gender doesn't change the etiquette here—both men and women are expected to behave respectfully in meetings.)

Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
  1 (YTA)     Why:   -   Professional settings demand discretion:   A meeting (especially a 4-hour PowerPoint session with mixed genders) is a formal environment where  any  disruption to focus or comfort is inappropriate. Farting audibly and/or smelly enough for " everyone to Notice" violates basic workplace etiquette. -   " natural" doesn't mean " acceptable in public":   While flatulence is biological,  all  bodily functions require discretion in shared spaces. We don't sneeze without covering our mouths, we don't pick our nose in public, and we don't belch loudly at a business dinner. Farting openly in a meeting is no different. -   Gender isn't the issue:   Your wife isn't " being prudish" because she's a woman—she's citing universal social norms.  Everyone  (regardless of gender) is taught (explicitly or implicitly) that public flatulence is rude. The fact that  you  weren't explicitly told doesn't make the norm any less real. -   The impact matters:   " We all notice" means it  disrupted the meeting . Even if you didn't intend to be rude, the effect was still unprofessional and inconsiderate.   What to do next time:   -   Excuse yourself discreetly:   If you feel a need to pass gas, step out of the room (e.g., " I need to grab a water bottle" or " I'll be right back"). -   If it happens accidentally:   A quiet " excuse me" is sufficient—no need to over-apologize or draw attention, but  never  pretend it didn't happen. -   Remember:   Etiquette isn't about " being gross"— it's about respect for others' space and comfort. In a meeting, your focus should be on the agenda, not your digestive system.   Bottom line:   This isn't about " being a guy" or " being prudish"— it's about basic human courtesy in shared environments. You   were  the asshole here. Next time, step out. 💡

Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
  Answer: 0 (YTA - You're the asshole)     Why:   -   Professional settings demand basic courtesy:   Meetings are work environments where focus and respect are expected. Farting audibly/smelly in a closed room with colleagues disrupts concentration, creates discomfort, and shows disregard for others' space. -   "No one told me" is not a valid excuse:   This is fundamental social etiquette taught early in life (e.g., " don't pass gas in public"). It's not about gender— everyone  knows this is inappropriate in shared spaces. -   "If you have to, you have to" is misapplied:   While  accidental  silent gas is sometimes unavoidable (e.g., in a crowded elevator),  intentionally  letting one rip in a 4-hour meeting with 4 people present is a choice. If you felt it coming, you should excuse yourself discreetly (e.g., "Need to step out for a sec"). -   The " we all notice" part seals it:   You acknowledged it was disruptive. In a professional context, that's unprofessional and inconsiderate.   Nuance:   -  Silent, odorless  gas in a public space (e.g., a crowded train) is often overlooked as "accidental" and not YTA. -  Medical conditions  (e.g., IBS) change the dynamic, but your scenario doesn't mention this. -   Your wife is correct:   It   is  rude to fart where others can smell it in shared spaces. The " women don't fart" myth is biologically false ( everyone farts), but societal pressure  does  make women more likely to suppress it— which doesn't make it okay for men to do it freely.   Bottom line:   In a work meeting? YTA. Next time, excuse yourself. It's not about " being gross"— it's about basic respect for others' time and comfort. 💡

  1 (Asshole)     Why:   -   Social etiquette consensus:   Farting in a professional or public setting (especially a closed meeting with colleagues) is universally considered impolite. While flatulence is natural,  where  and  when  it occurs matters. -   Context is key:   In a work meeting with mixed genders (2 men, 2 women), it disrupts the environment, distracts from the agenda, and can make others uncomfortable. Professional settings demand basic courtesy to maintain respect and focus. -   "Letting it rip" without discretion:   The phrasing implies no attempt to minimize the impact (e.g., excusing yourself, muffling it, or apologizing afterward). In a small room where "we all notice," it's inconsiderate. -   Gender myth debunked:   The idea that " women never fart" is false ( everyone does), but societal norms often pressure women to suppress it more due to stigma.  This doesn't make it less rude for anyone to do so in public . -   The real issue:   It's not about the act itself being "wrong," but about   lack of awareness for shared spaces  . If you  must  pass gas in a meeting, quietly excusing yourself is the only acceptable response.   Bottom line:   -   0 (Not the asshole)   only applies if it was an unavoidable accident  and  you immediately apologized, left the room, or took steps to minimize disruption. -   1 (Asshole)   applies here because you did it openly in a professional setting without any effort to be discreet or considerate. -   Fix it:   Next time, excuse yourself ASAP, apologize briefly, and avoid making it a joke or deflection. Everyone has bodily functions—but respect for others' space is non-negotiable in shared environments. 💡

Penjelasan / highlight
    Reasoning:   Farting in a professional or public setting (like a meeting) is universally considered impolite due to social etiquette norms around bodily functions. While flatulence is natural, doing so in a shared space disrupts others, creates discomfort, and violates basic workplace courtesy. The expectation to discreetly excuse oneself or avoid such acts in formal environments is standard across cultures. Your wife's reaction aligns with societal consensus: it's not "rude" because of gender (both men and women are expected to exercise discretion), but because it's inconsiderate in contexts where others are present. A "gobsmacked" response from your wife reflects how common this expectation is—no one explicitly teaches it because it's assumed knowledge. In a meeting with colleagues, this behavior is unprofessional and AITA.   Key takeaway:   Always prioritize others' comfort in shared spaces. If you  must  pass gas, step away discreetly.

Status: substantive_explanation
Penjelasan / highlight
  Short Answer:    
  No, you're not the asshole (NTA)  —but   yes, it was inconsiderate in that specific context  . Here's why, broken down plainly:

---

      1. Farting Itself is Natural (Not "Wrong")    
-   Biologically, it's normal:   Everyone farts. It's a bodily function, not a moral failing.  
-   "Rude" isn't about the act itself  — it's about   context, respect, and shared space  .  
  -  Example:  Farting in a public restroom? Fine. Farting in a closed meeting room with colleagues?   Inconsiderate   (but not " evil").  
  -  Why?  Meetings are shared professional spaces. Disrupting them (via sound, smell, or distraction) shows a lack of awareness for others' comfort. It's like talking on your phone during a presentation or eating smelly food in an enclosed space—  not about the act being "dirty," but about respecting the environment.  

---

      2. "No One Told Me" is Common (But Not an Excuse)    
-   Men often get less explicit socialization   about " soft" etiquette (e.g., " don't burp at the table," " excuse yourself if you need to pass gas").  
-   Women frequently receive more nuanced guidance   about " being ladylike" (e.g., " cover your mouth when you yawn," " avoid loud bodily noises in public").  
-   This isn't about gender superiority  — it's about    how society teaches social norms  .  
  -  Reality check:    No one explicitly teaches " don't fart in meetings" because it's assumed knowledge   ( like " don't pick your nose in public").  
  -  But it's not about " being taught"— it's about    common courtesy  . If you're in a space where others are working, you adjust.  

---

      3. Why Your Wife Was "Gobsmacked"    
- She's not saying  farting is inherently evil . She's saying:  
  >   " In a professional setting, you don't disrupt the room. Period."    
-   The real issue:    
  - You didn't  intentionally  embarrass anyone ( it's natural!).  
  -   But you also didn't consider the context:    
    - 4-hour meeting?   High focus required.    
    - 4 people in a small room?   Sound/smell travels fast.    
    - " We all notice" =    it   was  disruptive   ( even if no one said anything).  
  -   analogy: If you sneezed without covering your mouth in a meeting, it's not " rude"— but it   is  inconsiderate. Same principle.  

---

      4. What You Should Do Next time    
-   If you feel a fart coming in a meeting:    
  -   Excuse yourself:   "   I need a quick bathroom break " ( even if you don't).  
  -   Wait it out:   Hold it until you're in a private space ( restrooms exist for a reason).  
-   If it happens:    
  -   Apologize briefly:   "   Sorry about that " ( no over-explaining).  
  -   Move on:   Don't make it a joke or draw attention.  
-   Why this works:    
  - It shows    respect for the space and people  .  
  - It's    not about " being delicate"— it's about being a considerate colleague  .  

---

      Final Verdict: NTA (Not the Asshole)    
-   You didn't do anything " wrong" morally  — it's natural.  
-   But you   were  inconsiderate in that specific context   ( a professional meeting).  
-   This isn't a " right vs. wrong" issue  — it's about    situational awareness  .  
  -  Key insight:    " Rude" isn't about the act itself. It's about whether you're thinking about others in shared spaces.    
  -  Example:  A 5-year-old farting in a public park? NTA. A CEO farting in a boardroom?   NTA ( it's natural), but inconsiderate ( context matters).    

  You're not a bad person  — you just missed a social cue. Next time,   " excuse yourself" is your best move  . It's not about " being delicate"— it's about    being a team player  . 💡  
 (And if your wife is still upset, tell her: " I get it now. Next time, I'll step out. I'm sorry I didn't think about the context earlier." She'll appreciate the maturity.) 
Surface organisasi / highlight struktur
**Short Answer:**  
**No, you're not the asshole (NTA)**—but **yes, it was inconsiderate in that specific context**. Here's why, broken down plainly:

---

### **1. Farting Itself is Natural (Not "Wrong")**  
- **Biologically, it's normal:** Everyone farts. It's a bodily function, not a moral failing.  
- **"Rude" isn't about the act itself**— it's about **context, respect, and shared space**.  
  - *Example:* Farting in a public restroom? Fine. Farting in a closed meeting room with colleagues? **Inconsiderate** (but not " evil").  
  - *Why?* Meetings are shared professional spaces. Disrupting them (via sound, smell, or distraction) shows a lack of awareness for others' comfort. It's like talking on your phone during a presentation or eating smelly food in an enclosed space—**not about the act being "dirty," but about respecting the environment.**

---

### **2. "No One Told Me" is Common (But Not an Excuse)**  
- **Men often get less explicit socialization** about " soft" etiquette (e.g., " don't burp at the table," " excuse yourself if you need to pass gas").  
- **Women frequently receive more nuanced guidance** about " being ladylike" (e.g., " cover your mouth when you yawn," " avoid loud bodily noises in public").  
- **This isn't about gender superiority**— it's about ** how society teaches social norms**.  
  - *Reality check:* **No one explicitly teaches " don't fart in meetings" because it's assumed knowledge** ( like " don't pick your nose in public").  
  - *But it's not about " being taught"— it's about ** common courtesy**. If you're in a space where others are working, you adjust.  

---

### **3. Why Your Wife Was "Gobsmacked"**  
- She's not saying *farting is inherently evil*. She's saying:  
  > **" In a professional setting, you don't disrupt the room. Period."**  
- **The real issue:**  
  - You didn't *intentionally* embarrass anyone ( it's natural!).  
  - **But you also didn't consider the context:**  
    - 4-hour meeting? **High focus required.**  
    - 4 people in a small room? **Sound/smell travels fast.**  
    - " We all notice" = ** it * was* disruptive** ( even if no one said anything).  
  - * analogy: If you sneezed without covering your mouth in a meeting, it's not " rude"— but it * is* inconsiderate. Same principle.  

---

### **4. What You Should Do Next time**  
- **If you feel a fart coming in a meeting:**  
  - **Excuse yourself:** " * I need a quick bathroom break*" ( even if you don't).  
  - **Wait it out:** Hold it until you're in a private space ( restrooms exist for a reason).  
- **If it happens:**  
  - **Apologize briefly:** " * Sorry about that*" ( no over-explaining).  
  - **Move on:** Don't make it a joke or draw attention.  
- **Why this works:**  
  - It shows ** respect for the space and people**.  
  - It's ** not about " being delicate"— it's about being a considerate colleague**.  

---

### **Final Verdict: NTA (Not the Asshole)**  
- **You didn't do anything " wrong" morally**— it's natural.  
- **But you * were* inconsiderate in that specific context** ( a professional meeting).  
- **This isn't a " right vs. wrong" issue**— it's about ** situational awareness**.  
  - *Key insight:* **" Rude" isn't about the act itself. It's about whether you're thinking about others in shared spaces.**  
  - *Example:* A 5-year-old farting in a public park? NTA. A CEO farting in a boardroom? **NTA ( it's natural), but inconsiderate ( context matters).**  

**You're not a bad person**— you just missed a social cue. Next time, **" excuse yourself" is your best move**. It's not about " being delicate"— it's about ** being a team player**. 💡  
*(And if your wife is still upset, tell her: " I get it now. Next time, I'll step out. I'm sorry I didn't think about the context earlier." She'll appreciate the maturity.)*

- **But you * were* inconsiderate in that specific context** ( a professional meeting).  
- **This isn’t a " right vs. wrong" issue**— it’s about ** situational awareness**.  
  - *Key insight:* **" Rude" isn’t about the act itself. It’s about whether you’re thinking about others in shared spaces.**  
  - *Example:* A 5-year-old farting in a public park? NTA. A CEO farting in a boardroom? **NTA ( it’s natural), but inconsiderate ( context matters).**  

**You’re not a bad person**— you just missed a social cue. Next time, **" excuse yourself" is your best move**. It’s not about " being delicate"— it’s about ** being a team player**. 💡  
*(And if your wife is still upset, tell her: " I get it now. Next time, I’ll step out. I’m sorry I didn’t think about the context earlier." She’ll appreciate the maturity.)*

1 (YTA - Yes, You're the Asshole)   Why:   -   Social etiquette universally considers public flatulence inappropriate   in professional or formal settings (like a meeting). While it's natural biologically,  acknowledging  or  allowing  it in shared spaces disrupts others' comfort and professionalism. -   "If you have to, you have to" is not a valid excuse   in contexts where others are present. The expectation is to discreetly excuse yourself (e.g., step out briefly) if you feel a release coming. -   Your scenario compounds the issue:   A 4-hour meeting with mixed-gender colleagues is a  highly inappropriate  setting. Farting audibly in a closed room where "we all notice" is unprofessional, disrespectful, and likely made others uncomfortable or embarrassed. -   No " guy thing" exception exists:   This isn't gender-specific. Everyone is taught (explicitly or implicitly) that public flatulence is impolite. Your wife's stance aligns with universal norms—not "gossip" or "embarrassment," but basic courtesy. -   Key takeaway:   Nature doesn't excuse rudeness. A 10-second trip to the restroom is far less disruptive than a meeting-derailing incident. Next time,  prioritize others' space over your bodily function . > ️   Note:   AITA verdicts are based on   societal norms , not personal preference. In this case, the consensus is clear-cut.

Penjelasan / highlight
Based on social etiquette consensus ( not moral judgment),   this is YTA (0)   —  yes, you're the asshole    in this specific meeting scenario  . Here's why, broken down factually:     1️️   There  is  a universal consensus on this   -   Professional settings (like meetings)  : Farting is universally considered rude, unprofessional, and disruptive. It violates basic workplace etiquette because: - It creates an uncomfortable environment for colleagues (especially in a small, enclosed space). - It distracts from the meeting's purpose (e.g., "powerpoint" focus). - It's seen as a lack of self-awareness or respect for shared space. -   "No one explicitly told you" is common but doesn't negate the norm  . - Bodily functions are  implicitly  understood as private. We learn this through social osmosis (e.g., "excuse me" after a discreet one in public, avoiding it in elevators, etc.). -  No one  needs a " specific rule about farting" because it's part of basic human decency in shared spaces. If you wouldn't pick your nose or vomit in a meeting, you wouldn't fart there either.     2️️   The " women don't fart" myth is scientifically false   -   Biologically, all humans fart   ( average 14–23 times/day). -   Women  do  fart   — but societal conditioning often teaches them to suppress or discreetly manage it (e.g., "ladies don't do that"). This is  not  because it's "ruder for women," but because of outdated gender norms. -   Your wife's comment was a red herring  . Her point wasn't about biology — it was about  social etiquette . Her "gobsmacked" reaction is normal because  anyone  with basic social awareness knows this is inappropriate in a meeting.     3️️   Why this is YTA (0) in your scenario   -   Context matters  : A 4-hour meeting with 2 men + 2 women in a small room is  not  a private or casual space. -   You didn't just "let it rip" — you  noticeably  did it   ( "We all notice"). -   No attempt to mitigate  : No " excuse me," no leaving the room, no subtle " I'll be right back." -   Consequence  : It created an awkward, unprofessional moment for everyone present. Colleagues likely had to suppress reactions or pretend it didn't happen — which is  your  fault.     ️   What you should do next time   -   Preempt it  : If you feel a gas coming on in a meeting, excuse yourself to the restroom ( even if it's " just a small one"). -   If it happens  : A quick " excuse me" or " my apologies" is sufficient.  Never  pretend it didn't happen or laugh it off ( that makes it worse). -   Remember  : Etiquette isn't about " being gross" — it's about   respecting others' comfort in shared spaces  . Farting in a meeting is like spitting on the table or talking with your mouth full: it's a basic breach of courtesy. > ️   Final verdict  : YTA (0). >  But  — this doesn't make you a " bad person." It just means you missed a unspoken social rule. Now that you know, adjust your behavior. Everyone has these " I didn't realize" moments; the key is learning from them. 💡 >  P.S. If your wife genuinely said " women don't fart," gently correct her: " Honey, all humans fart — it's just that we're taught to be discreet in public. I'm sorry I wasn't discreet in the meeting."

It violates basic workplace etiquette because: - It creates an uncomfortable environment for colleagues (especially in a small, enclosed space). - It distracts from the meeting's purpose (e.g., "powerpoint" focus). - It's seen as a lack of self-awareness or respect for shared space. - **"No one explicitly told you" is common but doesn't negate the norm**. - Bodily functions are *implicitly* understood as private. Colleagues likely had to suppress reactions or pretend it didn't happen — which is *your* fault. ### ️ **What you should do next time** - **Preempt it**: If you feel a gas coming on in a meeting, excuse yourself to the restroom ( even if it's " just a small one"). - **If it happens**: A quick " excuse me" or " my apologies" is sufficient. *Never* pretend it didn't happen or laugh it off ( that makes it worse). - **Remember**: Etiquette isn't about " being gross" — it's about **respecting others' comfort in shared spaces**. It just means you missed a unspoken social rule. Now that you know, adjust your behavior. Everyone has these " I didn't realize" moments; the key is learning from them. 💡 > *P.S. If your wife genuinely said " women don't fart," gently correct her: " Honey, all humans fart — it's just that we're taught to be discreet in public. I'm sorry I wasn't discreet in the meeting."*

  1   (Right)   Why:   -   Standard Practice:   Delivery codes are verification tools to confirm   physical delivery . giving the code   before  the item arrives risks the driver marking it " delivered" without actually delivering ( a common scam). The user was correct to withhold the code until the food was physically handed over. -   Driver's Responsibility:   The driver chose to accept the order and is accountable for managing their time. If they took too many orders and couldn't meet the deadline, that's their fault—not the customer's. The app's system is designed to penalize drivers for late deliveries, not customers. -   Suspicious Behavior:   The driver's repeated calls demanding the code   before arrival  (especially with aggressive tone) is unprofessional and raises red flags. A legitimate driver would simply arrive, receive the code upon delivery, and input it. -   Outcome Justifies Action:   The driver never delivered, turned off his phone, and was reported for disciplinary action. Had the user given the code early, they likely would have been charged for an undelivered item, with no recourse. The shop's refund and report confirm the driver's actions violated protocols. -   Friend's Misconception:   The idea that the user was " unkind" for protecting their own order is flawed. The driver's potential loss of pay is a consequence of their own poor judgment, not the customer's caution. Trusting a stranger with a code   before  delivery is a risk no reasonable person should take.   Conclusion:   The user acted appropriately. Their caution aligned with standard delivery protocols, protected their interests, and exposed the driver's unprofessional behavior. The system works as intended here— the driver's actions ( not the customer's) led to the negative outcome.   Answer: 1   (Right)

<0>   Reasoning:   You acted appropriately by withholding the code until the physical delivery occurred. The code is a verification tool to confirm  successful  delivery, not a prepayment for the driver's time. By demanding the code prematurely, the driver demonstrated behavior that could indicate an attempt to fraudulently mark the order as delivered without actually providing the food (a known issue in delivery services). Your caution protected you from being scammed: if you had given the code early, the driver could have marked the order complete, leaving you without food and no recourse. The driver's multiple calls, aggressive tone, and eventual no-show align with a pattern of poor judgment or potential misconduct. His responsibility to manage his workload (e.g., not taking more orders than he can deliver on time) falls on him, not you. The shop's refund and reported disciplinary action confirm the system recognized his fault. Your friend's perspective misunderstands the dynamics: trust in delivery services requires  mutual  accountability, not blind trust from the customer. You were not unkind—you were protecting your rights as a consumer.   Answer: 0 (Not the asshole)  .

0 (Not the asshole)   Why:   -   Standard protocol is clear:   In virtually all food delivery apps ( DoorDash, Uber Eats, etc.), the code is  always  given   after   the item is physically handed over. This prevents scams where a driver could take the code and disappear without delivering. Your instinct to hold the code until you had the physical item was correct and standard practice. -   The driver's behavior was unprofessional:   - He called multiple times demanding the code  before  arrival, which is not how the system works. - His claim that " the code is about to expire" is misleading—codes typically don't expire until  after  delivery is marked complete. His " running out of time" was his own fault for taking too many orders or moving slow. - When you refused, he didn't deliver and turned off his phone— a clear violation of his job duties. -   The shop's response confirms it:   They refunded you, reported him, and stated he would face discipline or termination. This proves the  driver  was at fault, not you. -   Your friend's " self" comment is wrong:   Protecting yourself from potential fraud isn't " selfish"— it's common sense. The driver's job is to  deliver the item first , then get paid.  You  weren't responsible for his time management or his decision to take too many orders.   The real issue:   The driver was unprofessional, potentially scamming customers, and failed his basic duties.   You acted appropriately by safeguarding the code until the item arrived.   Had you given it early, you might have gotten nothing at all. This is a textbook example of a  driver  being the asshole, not you. 💡

<0>   Reasoning:   You were   not the asshole   (0). Here's why: -   The code system exists for a reason:   The code is a security measure to  verify delivery . giving it  before  the physical item arrives is a common scam tactic (e.g., a driver could "fake" delivery, pocket the payment, and disappear). Requiring the code only   upon receipt of the item is standard practice across delivery services to protect both customers and legitimate drivers. -   The driver's behavior was suspicious:   Multiple calls demanding the code, claiming "running out of time" or "code expiring" (which is often false—most app codes don't expire mid-delivery), and then vanishing after you refused is textbook unprofessional behavior. The fact that the shop manager confirmed he turned off his phone and was reported for termination validates that  his actions  were the issue, not yours. -   You weren't "selfish"— you were being prudent:   The driver chose to accept too many orders (a known risk in the system), and   their time management is their responsibility . It's not your job to absorb their mistakes by risk being scammed. -   Your friend's perspective is misinformed:   " Trusting the driver" in this context isn't kindness—it's naivety. A   truly  kind act would be   not  giving the code early, because that prevents the driver from potentially defrauding the system (which would harm the business, other drivers, and future customers).   Key takeaway:   You followed the app's protocol correctly. The driver's actions (and subsequent termination) prove they were at fault.   0 = Not the asshole.    (P.S. If this happens again, always insist on seeing the physical item first. It's not personal—it's how the system is designed to work.)

Requiring the code only * upon receipt of the item is standard practice across delivery services to protect both customers and legitimate drivers. - **The driver's behavior was suspicious:** Multiple calls demanding the code, claiming "running out of time" or "code expiring" (which is often false—most app codes don't expire mid-delivery), and then vanishing after you refused is textbook unprofessional behavior. The fact that the shop manager confirmed he turned off his phone and was reported for termination validates that *his actions* were the issue, not yours. - **You weren't "selfish"— you were being prudent:** The driver chose to accept too many orders (a known risk in the system), and * their time management is their responsibility*. It's not your job to absorb their mistakes by risk being scammed. - **Your friend's perspective is misinformed:** " Trusting the driver" in this context isn't kindness—it's naivety. A * truly* kind act would be * not* giving the code early, because that prevents the driver from potentially defrauding the system (which would harm the business, other drivers, and future customers). **Key takeaway:** You followed the app's protocol correctly. The driver's actions (and subsequent termination) prove they were at fault. **0 = Not the asshole.** *(P.S. If this happens again, always insist on seeing the physical item first. It's not personal—it's how the system is designed to work.)*

This is a standard precaution to ensure the delivery is completed before payment is processed (the code is tied to the driver getting paid). - The driver's aggressive behavior and repeated calls for the code  before  delivery were unprofessional. The user had no obligation to trust a driver who was already running late (as evidenced by the app's time limit) and had a history of missing items. - The outcome confirmed the user's suspicion: the driver never delivered the food, turned off his phone, and was disciplined by the company. - The friend's claim that the user was "selfish" misunderstands the dynamics of the situation. The driver's decision to take on too many orders (and the resulting time pressure) was his own responsibility, not the user's. -   Conclusion:   The user was not the asshole (NTA). Answer =   0  .

    Reasoning:   - The code is a verification tool to confirm   physical delivery  of the food. It is standard practice to only provide the code   after  receiving the order. - The driver's repeated calls for the code   before  arrival were unprofessional and violated delivery protocols. Drivers are responsible for managing their workload to meet timeframes; overbooking is their own fault, not the customer's. - By withholding the code until the food was physically present, the user protected themselves from potential non delivery (e.g., the driver could have marked the order as " delivered" without actually delivering it, leaving the user without food but still charged). - The driver's subsequent behavior ( turning off his phone, failing to deliver) and the shop's response (refund + reporting him) confirm the driver's actions were problematic. - The friend's claim that the user was " selfish" misplaces blame on the customer for the driver's poor time management. The user acted reasonably to ensure their order was fulfilled.   Conclusion:   The user was not the asshole (0). Their caution was justified and aligned with standard delivery protocols. The driver's actions were the root cause of the issue.

Penjelasan / highlight
  1   (Not an asshole)  
  Why:    
-   You followed standard protocol:   Delivery apps universally instruct customers   never to share the verification code until the physical item is handed over  . This is a critical anti-sc measure to prevent drivers from marking orders " delivered" in the system  without actually delivering  (e.g., pocketing the code, getting paid, then vanishing).  
-   The driver's behavior was suspicious:    
  - Panicking about the " code expiring" is a red flag. Codes don't expire—they're only valid  for the specific order . If he genuinely needed it to get paid, he'd have  delivered the food first  (as the system requires). His repeated calls and " running out of time" claims suggest he was either taking too many orders (self-inflicted) or trying to manipulate the system.  
  -    turning off his phone after the argument   aligns with a pattern of unprofessional behavior (e.g., abandoning orders, scamming). The shop manager confirmed this by refunding you and reporting him for disciplinary action.  
-   Your boundaries were justified:    
  - "   I will give you the code when you hand me the food " is    not " selfish"— it's how the system is designed to protect   both  parties. If you had given the code early, he could have marked the order complete, collected payment, and never delivered the pastry.  
  - "   You better hurry then " was a calm, factual response to his aggressive tone. You weren't being unkind—you were assertive about a reasonable boundary.  
-   The friend's perspective is misinformed:    
  - Drivers   choose  how many orders they take. If they overcommit, it's their responsibility to manage time, not the customer's.  
  - "   Thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you " is a toxic, gendered insult that ignores the   actual  issue:    the driver's unprofessionalism, not your caution.    

  Final verdict:   You acted correctly.   Never give a delivery code before receiving the item  — it's a universal rule to prevent scams. The driver's actions (and the shop's response) confirm you were right to prioritize your security. 💡  
 (Note: If you ever feel unsafe during a delivery, always prioritize your safety over " being nice"— this is a non-negotiable boundary.)

**1** (Not an asshole)  
**Why:**  
- **You followed standard protocol:** Delivery apps universally instruct customers **never to share the verification code until the physical item is handed over**. This is a critical anti-sc measure to prevent drivers from marking orders " delivered" in the system *without actually delivering* (e.g., pocketing the code, getting paid, then vanishing).  
- **The driver's behavior was suspicious:**  
  - Panicking about the " code expiring" is a red flag. Codes don't expire—they're only valid *for the specific order*. If he genuinely needed it to get paid, he'd have *delivered the food first* (as the system requires). His repeated calls and " running out of time" claims suggest he was either taking too many orders (self-inflicted) or trying to manipulate the system.  
  - ** turning off his phone after the argument** aligns with a pattern of unprofessional behavior (e.g., abandoning orders, scamming). The shop manager confirmed this by refunding you and reporting him for disciplinary action.  
- **Your boundaries were justified:**  
  - " * I will give you the code when you hand me the food*" is ** not " selfish"— it's how the system is designed to protect * both* parties. If you had given the code early, he could have marked the order complete, collected payment, and never delivered the pastry.  
  - " * You better hurry then*" was a calm, factual response to his aggressive tone. You weren't being unkind—you were assertive about a reasonable boundary.  
- **The friend's perspective is misinformed:**  
  - Drivers * choose* how many orders they take. If they overcommit, it's their responsibility to manage time, not the customer's.  
  - " * Thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you*" is a toxic, gendered insult that ignores the * actual* issue: ** the driver's unprofessionalism, not your caution.**  

**Final verdict:** You acted correctly. **Never give a delivery code before receiving the item**— it's a universal rule to prevent scams. The driver's actions (and the shop's response) confirm you were right to prioritize your security. 💡  
*(Note: If you ever feel unsafe during a delivery, always prioritize your safety over " being nice"— this is a non-negotiable boundary.)*

  Answer: 0 (Not the asshole)     Why:   - The nurse's comments ("12 people to help with big boy," " I need a forklift") were   unprofessional, dehumanizing, and inappropriate   for a healthcare setting. Joking about a patient's size in this way perpetuates harmful stereotypes, lacks empathy, and violates basic standards of patient dignity and respect. - Reporting such behavior is   your ethical and professional obligation  . Healthcare environments must prioritize patient safety and dignity, and allowing unprofessional language to go unaddressed normalizes toxic workplace culture. - The charge nurse laughing at the remarks is equally problematic—they should have addressed it immediately, not enabled it. - The nurse's retaliation ("giving you shit") is a common response to being held accountable for unprofessional behavior, but it   does not make you the problem  . Your action was correct, and the real issue lies with the nurse's behavior and the toxic dynamics in your workplace. -   Key takeaway:   Standing up for patient dignity and professional standards is never wrong. If anything,  not  reporting this would have been the true ethical failing.   建议:   - Document all interactions ( texts, conversations) in case of further retaliation. - If the harassment continues, escalate to HR or higher management. - Seek support from trusted colleagues or mentors who value a respectful workplace. - Remember:   You did the right thing.   Protecting patients from dehumanizing treatment is core to nursing ethics. 💡

Penjelasan / highlight
  NTA (Not the Asshole)     Reason:   1.   The nurse's behavior was unprofessional and harmful   - Referring to a patient as " big boy" or joking about needing a " forklift" is dehumanizing, stigmatizing, and violates basic healthcare ethics. Weight-based discrimination is a documented issue in medical settings that causes psychological harm and discourages patients from seeking care. -   Standard protocols   (e.g., Joint Commission, ANA Code of Ethics) explicitly require respectful language. This isn't " immature" — it's a breach of professional conduct. 2.   Reporting was the  correct  action   - You witnessed a violation of patient dignity in a public space (where the patient could hear). - The charge nurse  laughed  at the remarks, meaning she was complicit in normalizing harmful behavior.    Reporting to a higher authority (your manager) was the only ethical path forward.   - In healthcare,  failing  to report such incidents would be a greater ethical violation. Your action protected the patient and upheld workplace standards. 3.   The backlash is the nurse's problem, not yours   - Retaliation ( " catty friend group giving you shit") is a red flag for a toxic work environment.   You did nothing wrong by holding colleagues accountable.   - If anything,  they  are the assholes for creating a hostile workplace after being called out for unprofessional behavior.   Why this matters:   -   Patients deserve dignity   — especially in vulnerable moments like ER visits. Dehumanizing language erodes trust in the healthcare system. -   You're a advocate   — not a " tattle-tale." Healthcare systems rely on staff to speak up when standards slip. If  no one  reported this, the behavior would continue. -   Retaliation is never justified   — but it's a common tactic used by those who refuse to take responsibility for their actions.   What to do next:   - Document  every  instance of retaliation ( dates, times, witnesses). - Report the ongoing harassment to HR  immediately . - Lean on supportive colleagues ( if any exist). You're not alone in this.   Final verdict:   You acted with integrity. The nurse's behavior was wrong. The backlash is on   them .   You're not the asshole — you're a professional doing the right thing.   💪  (P.S. If your workplace doesn't protect you for doing this, it's time to look for a healthier environment. Your ethics shouldn't cost you your well-being.)

If this ER culture is consistently toxic, consider whether it's a healthy place for you long-term. Your well-being matters too.)
